questions.question_stem: A group starts with a simple append-only activity log. Which set of additions most directly turns it into a distributed ledger for untrusted multi-party coordination?
questions.correct_answer: Replicate the log, hash-link entries for tamper evidence, and use consensus to agree on ordering.
incorrect_answers: Replicate the log across partners, encrypt entries, and let an administrator decide conflicts.
Hash-link entries on one server, add audit exports, and resolve conflicting writes by review.
Give participants local copies, reconcile monthly, and allow approved edits to rewrite history.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames distributed ledgers as an upgrade from logs through replication, cryptographic hash-linking, and consensus over a shared sequence.

questions.question_stem: Two independent participants submit conflicting updates to a shared record at about the same time. In a distributed ledger, what mechanism is responsible for establishing the accepted sequence?
questions.correct_answer: Consensus rules determine which ordering the network treats as authoritative.
incorrect_answers: Hash-linking orders updates by comparing their resulting block hashes.
Replication resolves conflicts by keeping first update each node received.
Access-control policy settles conflicts by hiding one submitter's update.
questions.explanation: Consensus is the mechanism that lets distributed nodes agree on one consistent ordering of events despite failures, conflicts, or malice.

questions.question_stem: A malicious operator changes an old ledger entry on one node but does not control the rest of the network. What should hash-linking and replication make likely?
questions.correct_answer: The altered entry breaks later hash commitments, and other replicas can expose the discrepancy.
incorrect_answers: The altered copy is accepted if the operator recomputes local hashes before replicas can compare.
The network treats the edit as a normal correction once the operator preserves the entry's timestamp.
Replicas keep matching because hashes verify each entry separately rather than chaining history.
questions.explanation: Hash-linking makes retrospective edits detectable because later entries depend on earlier hashes, and replication lets other participants compare against unchanged copies.

questions.question_stem: A company needs a high-throughput internal inventory system controlled by one trusted owner, with frequent corrections and complex queries. Which architecture best matches the tradeoffs involved?
questions.correct_answer: A centralized database, because the trust model has one accountable owner and performance matters more than distributed finality.
incorrect_answers: A permissioned ledger, because internal validators could improve auditability even though one company already controls the workflow.
A permissionless ledger, because outside validators could replace the company's trusted inventory administrator and provide public audit.
A replicated append-only audit log, because preserving inventory history should take priority over frequent corrections and queries.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that a ledger is not a universal upgrade. If a single trusted owner can administer the system and performance/query flexibility are central, a centralized database is usually the better fit.

questions.question_stem: A consortium of banks wants a shared settlement record. Members are known, access must be controlled, and entries should become final once ordered by the agreed process. Which design is most appropriate?
questions.correct_answer: A permissioned ledger with curated membership, explicit governance, and deterministic finality.
incorrect_answers: A permissionless ledger with open validators, token incentives, and probabilistic settlement.
A centralized clearing database run by one bank, with that operator setting final order.
Bilateral private logs, with each bank reconciling periodically outside a common ordering service.
questions.explanation: Permissioned ledgers fit scenarios with known participants, access control, policy-driven governance, and deterministic finality.

questions.question_stem: Why does a permissionless ledger need a sybil-resistance mechanism such as economic or computational cost?
questions.correct_answer: Because open membership would otherwise let one actor cheaply create many identities and distort consensus.
incorrect_answers: Because open networks use the cost mainly to keep transaction contents private from non-validator observers.
Because the cost lets each node accept its own fork without needing agreement from the rest of the network.
Because it turns anonymous participation into deterministic finality as soon as one block is proposed.
questions.explanation: Permissionless systems are open to anyone, so they cannot rely on admission control alone. Sybil resistance makes fake mass participation costly.

questions.question_stem: A stakeholder says, "The ledger is immutable, so old records are physically impossible to alter." What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: Ledger immutability means tampering is detectable and reversals become difficult because of hash chains, replication, and consensus finality.
incorrect_answers: Ledger immutability means historical records can be corrected by replacing the affected block and reusing the same later hash values.
Ledger immutability means replicas keep backups, so an administrator can select which edited copy becomes the canonical history.
Ledger immutability means consensus finality protects history even when entries are not cryptographically linked to prior records.
questions.explanation: The lesson deconstructs immutability as tamper-evidence plus finality, not as a magical physical impossibility of alteration.

questions.question_stem: A hospital rejects ledger-based auditing because it assumes transparency means every patient's data must be public. Which response best addresses this misconception?
questions.correct_answer: Transparency can mean verifiability of rules and state, while private payloads remain protected by access controls or cryptographic techniques.
incorrect_answers: Transparency mainly means publishing clinical payloads to validators, with patient privacy handled through off-ledger contracts and hospital policy.
Privacy can be preserved by storing hashes of records, because hashes give auditors enough raw details for review, reporting, and compliance.
Integrity audits should be done outside the ledger, because validation and confidential records are separate compliance goals for hospitals.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates transparency from privacy: systems can make integrity and rule compliance verifiable without exposing all sensitive data.

questions.question_stem: A merchant accepts payment on an open permissionless ledger. Why might the merchant wait for additional blocks before releasing goods?
questions.correct_answer: Finality is probabilistic, so confidence that the payment will remain in the accepted history increases as more blocks build on it.
incorrect_answers: Finality is deterministic, so the merchant waits until a fixed committee formally certifies the payment in writing before goods release.
Additional blocks improve confidentiality, so waiting keeps the payment amount hidden from outside observers and merchants.
The first block is a local memo, and the payment is broadcast to the network only after later blocks are accepted by validators.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts probabilistic finality in many permissionless systems with deterministic finality often found in permissioned systems.

questions.question_stem: A design team wants to maximize decentralization by adding many independent validators across organizations. Which tradeoff should they expect?
questions.correct_answer: More distributed trust and fewer concentrated control points, but greater coordination overhead and likely higher latency.
incorrect_answers: Lower latency and simpler coordination, because more validators can divide ordering decisions across parallel consensus groups.
Stronger payload privacy, because validator diversity keeps transaction contents hidden from participating nodes.
Less governance complexity, because no single validator can decide upgrades or dispute outcomes for the network.
questions.explanation: The lesson's central tradeoff is that decentralization distributes trust and reduces concentrated power, but introduces overhead, latency, and governance complexity.

questions.question_stem: Consider institutions that each maintain separate databases and update one another through messages. What reconciliation problem can a distributed ledger reduce?
questions.correct_answer: Participants can verify shared data or proof points so they can detect when their records diverge.
incorrect_answers: Each institution keeps its database unchanged and treats email confirmations as the shared source of truth.
Participants stop comparing records because replication makes each local update valid network-wide.
Administrators resolve mismatches by editing peer records after disputes appear in separate systems.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes reconciliation through cryptography: multiple parties can verify that copies or proof points match rather than relying only on separate message-based updates.

questions.question_stem: A project lead claims that because the ledger uses strong cryptography, its deployment no longer needs security review. Which response is strongest?
questions.correct_answer: Strong cryptography can still be bypassed through keys, wallets, software defects, hardware weaknesses, validators, or user behavior.
incorrect_answers: Security review can focus only on cryptographic algorithms, since validator operations and key storage are outside the ledger threat model.
Strong cryptography removes update planning when validators use permissioned identities and approved operational software.
The main deployment risk is user misunderstanding, rather than compromise of keys, software, hardware, or validator operators.
questions.explanation: The reading stresses that ledger security is a full-system concern. Key management, wallets, software, hardware, validators, users, updates, and testing remain important even when cryptographic primitives are strong.

questions.question_stem: A government official rejects distributed ledgers because they associate the term only with Bitcoin. Which statement best complicates that view?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin is one unpermissioned application, while distributed ledger technology is a broader family for shared institutional records, provenance, identity, and public services.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin is one public network, while distributed ledger technology is simply a backup strategy for institutions that keep separate databases and reconcile records by email.
Bitcoin is the reference template, so serious distributed ledger projects should keep open mining, public token incentives, proof-of-work validation, and probabilistic finality.
Bitcoin is one cryptocurrency, while distributed ledger technology mainly means national token systems for payment modernization, trading, and fiscal reporting.
questions.explanation: The reading frames distributed ledgers as broader shared record-keeping infrastructure and uses public-sector and provenance examples to move beyond treating DLT as a synonym for Bitcoin.
